sections.overview: The goldcrest is one of Europe’s smallest birds, a restless, tiny insect-eater of conifer woods. Its numbers swing with the severity of winter, and large clutches help it recover from the heavy losses cold weather causes.
sections.identification: It weighs only 5–6 g and is about 9 cm long. The body is dull greyish-green with a pale belly, a large dark eye in a pale eye ring, two white wing bars and a thin bill. A yellow crown stripe bordered with black is orange in the male and yellow in the female; juveniles lack the stripe.
sections.habitat: In the breeding season it is most frequent in coniferous woodland, and it also uses mixed woods, parks and gardens with mature trees, mostly staying in the treetops. In winter it moves lower, into hedges and scrub.
sections.diet: It is mainly insectivorous, picking small invertebrates such as insects and spiders from foliage, especially conifer needles, and often hanging upside down while it hunts.
sections.behavior: It is very active and restless, and its high-pitched, repetitive song is the best way to find it. In winter it often joins roaming flocks of tits. Autumn brings arrivals from Scandinavia and Russia, which boost winter numbers in Britain.
sections.reproduction: In Britain the first clutch is laid around early May and there are typically two broods. A clutch is typically six to eight eggs and can reach twelve. The female alone incubates for about 16–19 days, and the downy chicks fledge after roughly 16.5–18 days. Breeding usually begins at one year.
sections.ecology: Cold winters are the main check on its numbers: RSPB reports that about eight in ten goldcrests die each winter. Predators include the Eurasian sparrowhawk and the pygmy owl. A typical bird lives about two years, and the oldest ringed one in Britain reached just over five.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern, and it is Green-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was estimated at 790,000 territories in 2016, though it fluctuates with winter weather, and numbers in Europe have declined since 1980.
